sentences.text: The tracks went up through the thin birch and across the shoulder of the hill and stopped at a hollow under a leaning rock, and the bear was in it.
She was asleep.
Tolek's first thought, which he was not proud of afterwards, was that she was much too big.
Everything he had been told about bears had been told to him by people describing bears, and describing is not the same as seeing.
She filled the hollow the way water fills a cup.
His second thought was that he was not frightened, and that this was strange, and that he should probably examine it later when he was somewhere else.
The cold was coming off her.
He could see it.
That is the part he could never explain properly, not to his mother and not to anyone since.
You know how heat comes off a road in August — that shiver in the air, that wobble?
It was that, but backwards, and going down instead of up.
It poured off her shoulders and pooled in the hollow and ran out over the lip of it, and where it ran, frost stood up on the grass in little white fences.
She was breathing.
Very slowly.
He counted, and it was nine seconds in and thirteen out, which is slower than seemed reasonable for something that size.
There was snow in her fur.
Not on it — in it, down between the hairs, right against the skin, and it was not melting even there.
When he finally came close enough to look properly he could see individual flakes, whole and six-sided and perfect, months old, held there as if the calendar had not been told.
He sat down at what he judged to be a polite distance, which was about four metres, on a stone that turned out to be very cold.
And sitting there, in the quiet, with the frost fences growing at his feet, he understood the thing that had brought him up the mountain, and it arrived complete, without anybody telling him.
She was not causing the winter.
She was holding it.
Somebody had to carry the cold from one year to the next.
It could not simply stop; it had to be taken somewhere and kept until it was needed again.
And the carrying was heavy — you only had to look at her to see how heavy — and she had been carrying it since October and she had not been able to put it down.
He did not know why she could not put it down.
He thought about it a great deal and never worked it out.
Some things are heavy for reasons that are nobody's business.
He went down before dark.
The tracks he made going down were the only tracks going down.
